start.text: Start here. Look at the fish's overall body plan.

options.label: Body eel-like or leech-like: no paired pelvic fins, and either a round jawless sucking mouth or a continuous fin margin with no true biting jaw
Normal fish body plan: paired pelvic fins present and a jawed mouth with a distinct upper/lower jaw
Round, jawless sucking disc mouth with no visible jaw, and a row of 7 small round gill openings behind the eye on each side
Small but normal jaw, a single covered gill opening on each side, well-developed pectoral fins, elongate snake-like body with a continuous dorsal-caudal-anal fin margin

result-sea-lamprey.note: If this is a small (5-15 cm), eyeless-looking, burrowing larva, it's an ammocoete — a very common but easily-missed electrofishing/kick-seine bycatch in silty stream margins, not a young eel.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Eel has a normal jawed mouth, one covered gill opening per side, and pectoral fins; lamprey has none of these.

result-american-eel.note: Check size/pigmentation to estimate life stage: transparent = glass eel, lightly pigmented = elver, olive-brown = yellow eel, silvery with a dark cape = silver eel (pre-migration).

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Ammocoetes are jawless with a hooded mouth and no externally visible eyes; eels have a normal small jaw and visible eyes.

has-adipose.text: Look at the back, between the dorsal fin and the tail.

options.label: A small, fleshy adipose fin is present (no rays or spine, just a soft flap)
No adipose fin — only the dorsal fin(s) and tail, nothing in between

adipose-group.text: Adipose-finned fish in Nova Scotia are the salmonids (salmon, trout, char) plus rainbow smelt and Atlantic tomcod. Check the mouth and body.

options.label: Small, slender, silvery fish (usually under 25 cm) with a single dorsal fin and either a chin barbel or prominent canine-like teeth on the tongue
Larger-bodied salmon/trout/char shape: no chin barbel, no strong tongue teeth, often spotted or patterned

smelt-tomcod-key.text: Check for a chin barbel and count the dorsal fins.

options.label: A single small barbel under the chin; three separate dorsal fins and two anal fins; upper jaw projects past the lower jaw; body heavier, mottled brown
No chin barbel; a single dorsal fin; slender iridescent silvery body with prominent canine-like teeth on the tongue and roof of the mouth; deeply forked tail

result-atlantic-tomcod.note: A small codfish relative of fresh/brackish tidal reaches.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Smelt has no chin barbel, only one dorsal fin, and strong tongue teeth; tomcod has a barbel, three dorsal fins, and no notable tongue teeth.

result-rainbow-smelt.note: Check for the adipose fin to confirm it isn't a young alewife/blueback herring, which never have one.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Tomcod has a chin barbel and three dorsal fins; smelt has neither.
Herrings have a sawbelly keel of scutes and no adipose fin; smelt has an adipose fin and no sawbelly keel.

options.label: Small juvenile (roughly under 15 cm) showing oval parr marks along the sides, not yet in full adult coloration
Adult-sized or otherwise showing clear adult coloration/pattern

parr-key-1.text: Look at the adipose fin colour and the upper jaw (maxilla) length relative to the eye.

options.label: Adipose fin shows a faint orange/red tint AND the upper jaw reaches close to or past the rear edge of the eye; red/orange spotting may already be visible
Adipose fin is plain grey with no orange/red tint (check the back and fins for vermiculations next)

parr-key-2.text: Look at the back and the lower fins.

options.label: Back shows pale, wavy, worm-like vermiculations; lower fins (pelvic/anal/pectoral) have a white leading edge backed by a black stripe
No vermiculations; 8-11 oval parr marks each about as wide as the eye or narrower; short maxilla not reaching past the rear of the eye; only 1-4 spots on the gill cover

result-parr-brown-trout.note: The maxilla-length and adipose-fin-colour contrast with Atlantic salmon parr is the standard field couplet fisheries biologists use for this trio.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Salmon parr has a plain grey adipose fin and a short maxilla that does not reach past the eye.
Brook trout parr shows back vermiculations and white-edged lower fins, which brown trout parr lacks.

result-parr-brook-trout.note: Vermiculations plus white-edged, black-striped lower fins are diagnostic for brook trout at any age.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Salmon parr never shows back vermiculations.
Brown trout parr lacks vermiculations and white-edged lower fins; its adipose fin often shows an orange tint instead.

result-parr-atlantic-salmon.note: If any of the three characters (adipose colour, maxilla length, gill-cover spots) don't line up cleanly, stop and mark unidentified rather than guessing — this trio is the single hardest field ID in Nova Scotia streams.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Brown trout parr has a longer maxilla and often an orange-tinted adipose fin.
Brook trout parr shows back vermiculations that salmon parr never has.

salmonid-adult-1.text: Look at the spot colour on the back and sides.

options.label: Light (white, cream, or yellowish) spots on a dark background — never pink or red — with a deeply forked tail
Spots are absent, or are dark/black, or are red/orange — continue to the next character

result-lake-trout.note: The most deeply forked tail of any Nova Scotia trout/salmon/char, paired with pale (never pink/red) spotting.

lookalikeCheck.species: Splake (lake trout x brook trout hybrid, where both are stocked)
lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Splake show an intermediate, moderately forked tail with a mix of vermiculations and pale spotting.

salmonid-adult-2.text: Look at the back for wavy markings, and the flank spots for a blue halo.

options.label: Dark olive-green wavy vermiculations on the back; red spots with bright blue halos on the flanks; belly pale yellow-orange to red; tail nearly square
No vermiculations — continue to the next character

result-brook-trout-adult.note: Nova Scotia's official provincial fish emblem.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Lake trout has pale spots only (no red/blue) and a deeply forked tail.
Brown trout lacks vermiculations and has a red-margined (not solid orange) adipose fin.

salmonid-adult-3.text: Check the spot size/halo colour, the adipose fin margin, and how far the upper jaw reaches.

options.label: Large dark spots with pale (not blue) halos, often extending onto the dorsal fin; adipose fin has a red/orange margin; maxilla extends well past the rear of the eye
None of the above — continue to the next character

result-brown-trout-adult.note: Introduced to Nova Scotia in the 1920s from German and Loch Leven hatchery stock.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Salmon has a short maxilla (not past the eye), a plain adipose fin, and a more deeply forked tail.
Brook trout has back vermiculations and blue-haloed red spots that brown trout lacks.

salmonid-adult-4.text: Check the caudal (tail) fin and the flanks for a stripe.

options.label: Dense small black spots covering the back, sides, dorsal fin, AND the caudal fin in rows; a broad pink-to-red lateral stripe

Few or no spots on the tail; silvery fresh from the sea, becoming bronze/brown with spots concentrated above the lateral line; no pink stripe; tail moderately to deeply forked, more square-edged in large fish

result-rainbow-trout.note: Mostly stocked/put-and-take in Nova Scotia; acid-sensitive, so wild reproduction is limited to a few Cape Breton systems.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Salmon lacks the pink lateral stripe and dense tail spotting.

result-atlantic-salmon-adult.note: Spawning males develop a hooked lower jaw (kype).

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Brown trout has a longer maxilla, pale-haloed dark spots, and a red-margined adipose fin.
Rainbow trout has a pink stripe and dense black tail spotting that salmon lacks.

options.label: Downward-pointing (subterminal), toothless, papillose sucking mouth with no barbels
Normal terminal or slightly angled jawed mouth

result-white-sucker.note: The only sucker species native to Nova Scotia — no sucker-vs-sucker confusion in this province.

bullhead-check.text: Look for barbels around the mouth and a spine at the front of each pectoral fin.

options.label: Four pairs of barbels (whisker-like) around the mouth, dark chin barbels, and a stout serrated pectoral spine
No barbels, or only a single small barbel — continue

result-brown-bullhead.note: Common in warm, weedy NS lakes and ponds.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Eel has no barbels, no adipose fin, no pelvic fins, and a continuous dorsal-caudal-anal fin margin.

stickleback-check.text: Look at the back just in front of the dorsal fin.

options.label: A row of separate, free spines (not webbed together into one fin) in front of a small soft dorsal fin
No free spines — continue

stickleback-count.text: Carefully count the free dorsal spines and check the tail base.

options.label: 6 or more (usually about 9) short free spines; a bony keel of scutes runs along the side of the caudal peduncle toward the dorsal fin
Only 2 to 4 (usually 3) stouter free spines; no scute keel at the tail base, though bony side plates may be present

result-ninespine-stickleback.note: Re-count the spines if in doubt — ninespine and threespine stickleback commonly co-occur in the same trap.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Threespine has only 2-4 stouter spines and a caudal keel of scutes rather than lateral plates.

result-threespine-stickleback.note: Both anadromous (sea-run) and resident freshwater forms occur in NS; lateral plating varies by population.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Ninespine has 6-12 shorter spines and a distinct caudal-peduncle keel that threespine lacks.

sculpin-check.text: Look at the head shape, scales, and pectoral fins.

options.label: Broad, flattened head tapering sharply to a slender body; no scales anywhere; large fan-like pectoral fins; two separate dorsal fins (a short spiny one and a soft one)
None of the above — continue

result-slimy-sculpin.note: Unmistakable among NS freshwater bycatch — no other species here has this scaleless, broad-headed body plan.

pickerel-check.text: Look at the snout and the dorsal fin position.

options.label: Long, flattened, duck-bill snout full of small sharp teeth; a single soft dorsal fin set far back near the tail, no separate spiny dorsal fin
Rounded snout, not a duck-bill — continue

result-chain-pickerel.note: Non-native and invasive in Nova Scotia — mandatory retention (do not release) has applied province-wide since April 1, 2025. Check current NS angling regulations for the latest rule.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Eel has no pelvic fins, no visible scales, and a continuous fin margin, unlike a pickerel's scaled body with separate paired and dorsal/anal fins.

two-dorsal-check.text: Look at the dorsal fin(s) on the back.

options.label: Two dorsal fins are present (one spiny, one soft), whether touching, notched, or fully separated
Only one dorsal fin, or a single soft dorsal fin with no true spines

dorsal-gap-check.text: Look at how the two dorsal fins connect.

options.label: Joined by only a shallow notch, not a full gap
Clearly and fully separated by a gap about as wide as the eye or more

bass-check.text: Check the upper jaw length, eye colour, and flank markings.

options.label: Upper jaw (maxilla) does NOT reach past the rear margin of the eye; red eye; faint vertical bars, no horizontal stripes; robust bronze-olive body
6-9 continuous dark horizontal stripes along silvery sides; two tooth patches at the back of the tongue

result-smallmouth-bass.note: Non-native and invasive in Nova Scotia; a mandatory-retention order applies in the Margaree watershed (incl. Lake Ainslie) and part of the LaHave River since 2024 — check current regulations.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Yellow perch has two fully separated dorsal fins (a real gap) versus smallmouth bass's shallow notch.

result-striped-bass.note: In Nova Scotia the only robust remaining spawning run is the Shubenacadie-Stewiacke system; handle with care, this population is COSEWIC-listed Endangered.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: White perch has no horizontal stripes and only one tooth patch on the tongue (striped bass has two).

perch-sunfish-check.text: Look at the body shape and the gill cover.

options.label: Small, round, deep-bodied sunfish shape with a dark opercular (gill cover) flap bordered by a bright orange-red crescent
More elongate body with 6-8 sharply defined dark vertical bars on a golden-yellow/brassy background; no orange-red gill-cover crescent

result-pumpkinseed.note: Native-vs-introduced status in Nova Scotia is unresolved in the app's current data — record the catch normally, but treat this as a species worth double-checking against current ACCDC/DFO records.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Yellow perch is more elongate with two well-separated dorsal fins; pumpkinseed has one continuous dorsal fin and the orange-red gill-cover crescent.

result-yellow-perch.note: Very common in NS lakes; can be locally overabundant.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Both have only a shallow dorsal-fin notch or a single dorsal fin, versus yellow perch's fully separated pair.

herring-check.text: Look along the belly midline and check the tail/shoulder.

options.label: A sharp, saw-toothed keel of modified scales along the belly between the pelvic and anal fins; a single dark spot behind the gill cover; deeply forked tail
No sawtooth belly keel — continue

herring-pair-check.text: This is alewife or blueback herring — a genuinely difficult field pair (up to ~16% misidentification even with these characters). If the fish can be briefly and safely examined, check the body cavity lining (peritoneum) colour and compare eye diameter to snout length.

options.label: Peritoneum white/pale; eye diameter clearly larger than snout length; slightly deeper body; back more blue-grey/greenish
Peritoneum black/sooty; eye diameter about equal to or smaller than snout length; back distinctly blue

result-alewife.note: In NS spring runs, alewife typically arrive about two weeks before blueback herring — run timing can be a secondary clue at a known site.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Blueback has a black peritoneum and a smaller eye relative to snout length; if unsure, note run timing and photograph.

result-blueback-herring.note: If the peritoneum couldn't be checked confidently, mark this pair as unidentified and photograph both flanks plus a close-up of the eye/snout.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Alewife has a white peritoneum and a larger eye relative to snout length.

killifish-check.text: Look at the mouth position and body markings.

options.label: Upturned (superior) mouth, flattened top of the head, narrow dark vertical bars on the body, no barbels, no lateral line
None of the above — continue

killifish-pair-check.text: Compare the caudal peduncle (just before the tail) and where the dorsal fin sits.

options.label: Slender caudal peduncle; dorsal fin set relatively far forward; crisp, regular, well-defined vertical bars in both sexes
Deep caudal peduncle; rounded tail; dorsal fin set farther back toward the tail; blotchier pattern, males with a small dark spot at the rear of the dorsal fin

result-banded-killifish.note: Freshwater lakes/ponds/slow streams, tolerating brackish margins.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Mummichog has a deeper caudal peduncle, a rounded tail, and a dorsal fin set farther back.

result-mummichog.note: Typical of salt marshes, tidal creeks, and estuaries rather than upstream freshwater sites.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Banded killifish is slimmer with a more forward dorsal fin and crisper, more regular bars.

golden-shiner-check.text: Look at the lateral line shape and belly.

options.label: A fleshy, scaleless keel along the belly between the pelvic and anal fins, AND a lateral line that bows sharply downward (decurved) toward the belly
Straight lateral line, no fleshy belly keel — continue

result-golden-shiner.note: The sharply decurved lateral line is not shared by any other small Nova Scotia minnow.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Common shiner has a straight lateral line and no belly keel.

barbel-check.text: Look closely in the corner of the mouth for a small barbel — it can be tiny or embedded.

options.label: A single small barbel is present in the corner of the mouth
No barbel at all; large, loose scales that fall off easily; terminal mouth; deeply forked tail often with a dark spot at its base; dark mid-dorsal stripe

result-common-shiner.note: Frequent bycatch in clear, cool creeks and small rivers.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Dace has a barbel and fine scales that common shiner lacks.
Chub has a barbel and a dorsal-fin-base black spot that common shiner lacks.

dace-chub-check.text: Look for a large mouth and dark spots at the dorsal and caudal fin bases.

options.label: Large mouth reaching back toward the eye; a large black spot at the front of the dorsal fin base AND a black spot at the base of the tail
Small mouth, slightly overhung by a pointed snout; fine scales; a dusky lateral stripe running from the snout through the eye to the tail base; no dorsal/caudal black spots

result-creek-chub.note: A habitat generalist, often dominating small disturbed or intermittent headwater streams.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Dace is smaller-mouthed with no dorsal/caudal black spots.
Shiner has no barbel at all.

result-blacknose-dace.note: In NS, documented mainly in Northumberland Strait and Bay of Fundy watersheds draining the Cobequid Mountains.

lookalikeCheck.distinguishingNote: Chub is larger-mouthed with a dorsal-fin-base black spot and a caudal spot.
Shiner has no barbel and much larger, loose scales.
